evidence_quotes.quote: To illustrate this framework, we developed and estimated a Sustainable Water Governance Index (SWGI) for the city of Salta, Argentina.

Low investments and failure to provide services to the poorest areas of the city were a constant during both the public and private periods, as was also reported in other parts of the country and the world [65,66].

Information needed to build the SWGI was collected by several means including literature retrieval (including local media), field visits, and semistructured interviews conducted with officials of the institutions related to water management between 2009 and 2011.

Water Needs obtained the maximum score; the company has a system by which a minimum drinking water allowance of 10 m3 is subsidized (via a government fund) to those households that demonstrate a combined income below the official poverty line.

Table 2 shows the results obtained for the SWGI of the city of Salta, Argentina, which was used as a practical example to illustrate the method. The governance of the entire system obtained 49 points (Table 2, bottom of column 9).

criterion_notes.c1: Unclear/nominal only: the paper studies macro-level sustainability governance of a municipal water and sanitation management system (WSMS) in Salta, Argentina. Although one sub-index of its Sustainable Water Governance Index (SWGI) is labeled Access, it only rescales institutional website quality (36.7%), the ratio of benchmark household water tariff to the official minimum wage (1.9%), and the statutory 10 m3/month poverty subsidy divided by census household size (87.7 L/p.d), without empirically examining actual household or community service coverage, connections, continuity, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2, this paper would satisfy Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because it explicitly examines institutional, regulatory, and governance features of Salta's WSMS (planning capacity across CoSAySa, ENRESP, and SRH, public audiences, information websites, and tariff/subsidy parameters). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NOT satisfied (narrow=no): the paper develops a normative macro-governance conceptual framework ('governance for sustainability') and aggregates broad institutional and participatory descriptors into a single city-level index, while mentioning 1998 privatization/renationalization only as unanalysed historical background and treating tariff share of minimum wage and the 10 m3 poverty-line subsidy solely as static scoring inputs rather than analysing how any rule-type mechanism governs service access. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded because it fails Criteria 4 and 5 (Exclusion 11).
criterion_notes.c3: Sections 1 and 2 are purely conceptual/theoretical, while Sections 3 and 4 contain descriptive and semi-quantitative empirical case-study data for Salta collected between 2009 and 2011 via institutional interviews, field visits, website evaluations, and secondary documents to compute the illustrative SWGI.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: the reported outcome is a normative, city-level composite governance score (SWGI = 49 on a 0-100 scale) and sub-scores for institutional planning, public audiences, and website quality. Even the Costs (1.9% of minimum wage) and Water Needs (87.7 L/p.d, calculated by dividing the formal 10 m3 monthly poverty allowance by the census average of 3.8 persons per household) indicators reflect formal policy parameters on paper rather than empirical measurements of household water/sanitation access, connection, supply reliability, actual expenditure burden, subsidy take-up, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5 (and Exclusion 11): the unit of analysis is a single municipal WSMS (city of Salta, n = 1 cross-section) used to illustrate composite index construction, and sample sizes/interview protocols are not reported in the main text. No exposure-outcome relationship linking a governance or legal factor to household or community service access can be identified.

study_design: Conceptual framework with illustrative single-city composite governance index case study (cross-sectional, semi-quantitative)
population_and_sample: Water and sanitation management system (WSMS) of the city of Salta, Argentina (city population >500,000; three local institutions assessed: CoSAySa, ENRESP, and SRH; number of interviewees not reported)
outcome: Sustainable Water Governance Index (SWGI) composite score (49 on a 0-100 scale) and sub-index scores for Access (67), Planning (58), and Participation (20)
rationale: Excluded (E04, Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2 and Criterion 5 / Exclusion 11). This paper proposes a theoretical framework of 'governance for sustainability' and illustrates it by constructing a composite Sustainable Water Governance Index (SWGI = 49/100) for the municipal WSMS of Salta, Argentina. First, its evaluated outcome is an aggregated, normative system-level governance score rather than empirical household or community water/sanitation access, connection, continuity, coverage, or exclusion (even its 'Water Needs' score of 100 merely divides the utility's nominal 10 m3/month poverty-subsidy rule by census average household size of 3.8 rather than measuring actual household water access or subsidy receipt). Second, under the 2026-10-13 narrow Criterion 2 clarification, the paper assesses macro-governance and institutional planning/participation rather than analysing how a rule-type legal, regulatory, tariff, or eligibility mechanism shapes service access. Third, even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded because it is a single-city composite indicator illustration with no identifiable exposure-outcome relationship linking a governance factor to service access (Criteria 4 and 5; Exclusion 11).
